title: Telemetry Sampling & Privacy‑Balanced Onboarding Guide
author: Aisha Patel
summary: Practical, operational playbook for onboarding enterprise tenants with telemetry sampling that balances observability needs, privacy requirements, and cost constraints.
content:
Purpose
This document explains a repeatable onboarding pattern for enterprise customers that need high-fidelity observability while honoring privacy constraints and cost budgets. It is intended for Customer Success engineers, SREs, and partner integration teams who run Redwood inference workloads in hosted, dedicated, or private environments.

Scope
- Applies to telemetry collected from production inference traffic: logs, traces, token-level telemetry, request/response payloads, and derived metrics.
- Covers sampling strategies, privacy filtering, acceptance criteria, telemetry assertions, and rollback triggers.
- Does not replace legal or Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA); engage Security/Legal for regulated customers.

Goals
1. Ensure minimum observability to meet tenant SLOs and onboarding acceptance tests.
2. Minimize PII exposure and customer privacy risk by design.
3. Keep telemetry cost predictable and within customer / internal budget.
4. Provide clear operational runbook for escalation and rollback.

Key Terms
- High‑fidelity sample (HFS): full request/response payload, token-level timing, and traces.
- Metric-only sample (MOS): aggregated metrics and sampled traces but no payload.
- Privacy‑filtered: payloads with PII redacted or pseudonymized.

Recommended sampling matrix
Use this matrix to pick an initial sampling configuration based on customer tier and regulatory needs. Adjust during the onboarding runway.

| Customer tier | Default initial sampling | Privacy posture | Typical rate (requests/day) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| Enterprise (regulated) | MOS + privacy-filtered HFS for canary | High: pseudonymize, redact | 0.1% HFS, 100% MOS | Use for PCI/PHI customers; review with Security |
| Enterprise (standard) | MOS + 1% HFS | Medium: redaction of known PII types | 1% HFS, 100% MOS | Good balance for SLAs + debugging |
| Growth/PLG | MOS | Low: redaction by default | 0% HFS, 100% MOS | Cost-conscious; escalate to HFS on incidents |

Guidelines for choosing sampling algorithm
- Deterministic reservoir sampling keyed by tenant_id + day for reproducibility.
- Priority-based sampling: elevate failed requests, high latency, or behavioral anomalies to HFS.
- Adaptive sampling: increase HFS during canary windows or after model upgrade events.

Privacy and PII handling
1. Default policy: redact known PII (SSNs, credit card numbers, unstructured PHI) from payloads before any HFS storage.
2. Use ephemeral pseudonymization when customer consents to richer telemetry. Store mapping in customer-managed KMS-backed vaults when required.
3. Tokenization logs: never store raw user-provided sequences for customers that opt out of raw telemetry. Use hashed prefixes for correlation.
4. Provide customers a telemetry expectations doc with clear opt-in/opt-out steps and retention windows.

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step)
1. Pre-onboarding: legal & security signoff for telemetry posture. Record consent level in tenant profile.
2. Define SLOs and acceptance criteria with customer (latency P50/P95, error rate, freshness of embeddings).
3. Baseline run: enable MOS for 7 days to collect metrics and establish normal ranges.
4. Canary window (7–14 days): enable priority-based 1% HFS for a small subset (0.5–2% traffic) and validate instrumentation.
5. Privacy validation: run redaction/pseudonymization tests against synthetic PHI fixtures.
6. Cost projection: run a 48‑hour HFS burst to estimate billing impact; record in tenant pricing sheet.
7. Go/No‑Go gates: must pass telemetry assertions (see below), security review, and cost approval.
8. Post‑go live: keep MOS enabled and scheduled HFS bursts for weekly quality checks.

Telemetry assertions (automated checks to run during acceptance)
- Coverage: 95% of routed requests produce metric envelopes and traces (MOS).
- Correlation: 100% of HFS samples have trace IDs that map to MOS metrics within 30s.
- Privacy: no raw PII found in HFS payloads for tenants with privacy opt-out. Run regex-based and ML-based detectors.
- Freshness: derived metrics and cost-attribution tags are visible in Redwood Console within 5m of ingestion.

Example sampling configuration (YAML)
```yaml
telemetry: 
  sampling_strategy: priority_adaptive
  default_metric_sample: 1.0         # 100% MOS (metrics + minimal traces)
  high_fidelity: 
    rate: 0.01                        # 1% HFS for canary by default
    triggers: [error, latency_p95_exceed, manual_tag]
  privacy: 
    redaction_profile: standard-2026
    pseudonymization: optional
  retention_days: 30
  owner: cs-integration-engineering@redwood.com
```

Example HFS JSON snippet (privacy‑guarded)
```json
{
  "request_id": "r-123456",
  "tenant_id": "t-abc",
  "trace_id": "trace-987",
  "payload": "<redacted>",
  "tokens_observed": 42,
  "latency_ms": 86,
  "sample_type": "HFS",
  "privacy_flags": ["pseudonymized"]
}
```

Operational playbook for incidents during onboarding
1. Detection: telemetry assertion failure alerts to CS/SRE channel.
2. Immediate action: reduce HFS rate to 0% for affected tenant, keep MOS at 100%.
3. Triage: run tool-assisted PII scan on most recent HFS window. If PII is found, follow the Sensitive Data Exposure Escalation (notify Security and Legal, preserve evidence, start customer notification timeline within 48h).
4. Recovery: re‑deploy privacy filter rule updates, run synthetic validation tests, and permit incremental HFS re‑enablement (start at 0.01%).
5. RCA: produce a short incident summary for the customer and an internal postmortem with action items and owners.

Escalation contacts and ownership
- Primary: CS Integration Lead — Aisha Patel (cs-integration@redwood.com)
- Secondary: Observability SRE — Liam Chen (sre-observability@redwood.com)
- Privacy Escalation: Security Analyst — Marcos Rivera (security-telemetry@redwood.com)

QBR & Health check integration
- Include telemetry baseline graphs in the go‑live QBR packet: MOS coverage, HFS sampling rate, privacy incidents (0 expected), and telemetry cost delta vs baseline.
- Suggested QBR cadence in first 90 days: weekly health reports for first month, biweekly for month 2–3, then monthly.
- Actionable metrics for QBRs: metric coverage %, median trace latency, number of HFS samples flagged for privacy review, and monthly telemetry spend by tag.

Documentation & APIs to use
- Telemetry Schema (internal): /docs/telemetry/schema-v2 (request via platform docs portal).
- Sampling control API (example): POST /admin/v1/telemetry/{tenant_id}/sampling
- Redaction rules repository: git://redwood/telemetry/redaction-rules  (access controlled)

Testing and validation matrix
- Unit tests: redaction rules must pass fixture suite for 200+ synthetic PII patterns.
- Integration tests: ensure MOS envelopes correlate with HFS samples across trace boundaries.
- Load test: run 48h of MOS + scheduled 1% HFS at production RPS; validate cost projection within 20% of estimate.

Common pitfalls & mitigations
- Overindexing on HFS early: keeps costs and privacy risk high. Mitigation: use MOS + targeted HFS triggers.
- Insufficient correlation keys: require tenant_id and request_hash in all envelopes.
- Drift in telemetry schema: enforce schema validations at ingest with automatic alerting.

Appendix: sample onboarding checklist (one‑page)
1) Legal/Security telemetry posture OK — checkbox
2) MOS enabled and baseline collected (7 days) — date: ________
3) Canary HFS configuration set (rate: __%) — window start: ________
4) PII redaction verification passed — tester: ________
5) Cost projection uploaded to tenant sheet — owner: ________
6) Go/No‑Go decision: ________ (CS lead, SRE, Customer)
